title: Book of Moses 1:33–38
speaker: Joseph Smith
venue: Revelation (Visions of Moses), later canonized in the Pearl of Great Price

quotes.excerpt: And worlds without number have I created; and I also created them for mine own purpose... And as one earth shall pass away, and the heavens thereof even so shall another come; and there is no end to my works, neither to my words.
quotes.note: A single divine speaker creates all the worlds. He is the originator of the series, not a member of it.

notes: Retagged in v2: MANY-WORLDS, not INFINITE-CHAIN. Plurality of worlds is not succession of Gods. This text is context for later chain teachings rather than evidence of them — and the interpretive move by which Pratt and Young later recruit it is itself the datum, logged on those entries.

title: Discourse, 30 January 1842
speaker: Joseph Smith
venue: Nauvoo, Illinois

quotes.excerpt: the God & father of our Lord Jesus Christ was once the same as the Son or Holy Ghost bo[th] having redeemed a world became the eternal God of that world he had a son Jesus Christ who redeemed this earth the same as his father had a world which made them equal & the Holy Ghost would do the same in his turn & so would all the Saints who inherited a Celestial glory so their would be Gods many & Lords many.
quotes.note: Father-referent and explicit: the Father was once as the Son is, redeemed a world of His own, and stands in a repeating series ("Gods many & Lords many"). Backward regress and forward progression are stated in one breath, with the Christological analogy already doing the argumentative work it will do again in the King Follett Discourse.

notes: Added in v2, and it revises the working claim that the Sermon in the Grove is Joseph Smith's only unambiguous Father-referent BACKWARD-EXPLICIT statement. This discourse predates it by nearly two and a half years and is quoted in the Joseph Smith Papers footnotes to the Bullock report of the King Follett Discourse (footnote 9), which is where this entry was found. Rated C pending confirmation of the reporter and the exact JSP document ID — verify before leaning on it, since the wording above is transcribed from the KFD annotation rather than read off the discourse page itself.

title: Book of Abraham 3:18–26; 4:1
speaker: Joseph Smith
venue: Published in Times and Seasons, Nauvoo; later canonized in the Pearl of Great Price

quotes.excerpt: If there be two spirits, and one shall be more intelligent than the other... they shall have no beginning; they existed before, they shall have no end, they shall exist after, for they are gnolaum, or eternal.
quotes.note: Eternal, uncreated intelligences — no beginning means no begetting.

quotes.excerpt: And then the Lord said: Let us go down. And they went down at the beginning, and they, that is the Gods, organized and formed the heavens and the earth.
quotes.note: Context rather than evidence: plural organizing Gods, with no statement of how those Gods came to be.

notes: The TRIPARTITE tag is dropped in v2. Abraham 3 asserts eternal intelligences and plural organizing Gods; it never articulates intelligence → spirit → body staging. Note too that "intelligences" and "spirits" are used interchangeably across 3:22–23, which cuts against reading a stage distinction into the chapter at all. The three-stage model is B. H. Roberts's later synthesis — filed separately.

title: Doctrine and Covenants 132:19–20, 63
speaker: Joseph Smith
venue: Revelation recorded at Nauvoo; first published 1852; canonized 1876

quotes.excerpt: ...which glory shall be a fulness and a continuation of the seeds forever and ever. Then shall they be gods, because they have no end... then shall they be above all, because all things are subject unto them.
quotes.note: Promises deification and continuing "seeds" without naming either the mechanism or the object. Nothing here says spirit children.

quotes.excerpt: ...they are ordained to bear the souls of men; for herein is the work of my Father continued, that he may be glorified.
quotes.note: On its plainest reading v. 63 addresses plural mortal wives bearing children in mortality.

notes: Downgraded in v2 from FORWARD-EXPLICIT to FORWARD-EUPHEMISM. This is deliberate and contestable: the explicit spirit-procreation reading is supplied by later interpreters — Pratt, the 1909 First Presidency, Ballard — not by the verse. Holding the canon itself to the strict standard is what makes the euphemism/explicit boundary load-bearing, and that boundary is where the whole taper story lives. The dependency is preserved: the explicit teachings that cite this text carry the explicitness themselves, and the citation links show it.

title: King Follett Discourse
speaker: Joseph Smith
venue: General Conference, Nauvoo

witnesses.note: Contemporaneous longhand; the base text for the standard versification.
Contemporaneous longhand; sole witness to the "all Gods" wording.
Highly abbreviated notes in Joseph Smith's own journal; does not record the deification passage.
Journal account; does not record the deification passage.

quotes.excerpt: God himself was once as we are now, and is an exalted man... God himself, the Father of us all, dwelt on an earth, the same as Jesus Christ himself did.
quotes.note: Referent is unambiguously the Father — "the Father of us all" — but the Father's mortality is established by analogy to Christ. The Christological analogy is the engine of the discourse, and Snow later runs the same engine. Retagged for the Father axis: “was once as we are now” is the mortal experience; “is an exalted man” is the attainment.

quotes.excerpt: you have got to learn how to be a god yourself... to be priests & Kings as all Gods has done— by going from a small degree to another from exaltation to ex[altation] (Clayton) / you have got to learn how to be a God yourself & be a K[ing] & God Priest to God same as all have done (Bullock)
quotes.note: Verification resolved, and it matters. Of the four accounts, only Clayton attests "as all Gods has done"; Bullock has the weaker "same as all have done" with no "Gods"; Richards and Woodruff do not record the passage at all. The familiar amalgam reading "the same as all Gods have done before you" therefore rests on a single witness, and smooths away a real divergence. Weight the INFINITE-CHAIN tag on this quote accordingly.

quotes.excerpt: The mind or the intelligence which man possesses is co-equal [co-eternal] with God himself... God never had the power to create the spirit of man at all. God himself could not create himself. Intelligence is eternal and exists upon a self-existent principle.
quotes.note: The strongest support in the corpus for organization over begetting, and in direct tension with the viviparous statements of 1909.

notes: Amalgamated texts — the 1855 History draft, Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith, and the April 1971 Ensign — are citations of these four witnesses, not independent originals, and are filed as such. Honest accounting on the backward direction: the King Follett Discourse teaches that the Father was mortal. The had-a-Father inference arrives ten weeks later in the Sermon in the Grove.

title: Nauvoo Expositor: “a plurality of Gods above the God of this universe”
speaker: The proprietors of the Nauvoo Expositor
office: Dissenting former members of the Church at Nauvoo
venue: Nauvoo Expositor, June 7, 1844, p. 2 col. 3 (“Resolutions”)

witnesses.scribe: Gordon A. Madsen, Sustaining the Law: Joseph Smith's Legal Encounters, 434 and nn. 30–38
witnesses.note: Quotes the charge in full with column-level citations to the issue.

quotes.excerpt: introduced false and damnable doctrines into the Church, such as a plurality of Gods above the God of this universe, and his liability to fall with all his creations; the plurality of wives, for time and eternity; the doctrine of unconditional sealing up to eternal life, against all crimes except that of shedding innocent blood.
quotes.note: The full charge, including the clause that usually goes missing. Two things the standard ellipsis hides. First, the regress charge is bundled into one sentence with polygamy and unconditional sealing, so it is an item in a bill of particulars rather than a free-standing theological complaint. Second, “and his liability to fall with all his creations” is a distinct and independently striking claim — that God could fall — which no other source in this dataset touches, and it is preserved here deliberately. As a hostile witness this is evidence about what was audible in Nauvoo, not about what Joseph Smith taught.

notes: Verified verbatim against Gordon A. Madsen's quotation with column-level citation in Sustaining the Law: Joseph Smith's Legal Encounters, 434 (nn. 30–38 cite Nauvoo Expositor, June 7, 1844, p. 2, cols. 3–4). The Internet Archive's copy of the single issue is page images with no text layer, so the newspaper itself could not be machine-collated; the column reference is Madsen's. The excerpt begins mid-sentence: the original reads “inasmuch as they have introduced…,” so the opening verb here is the paper's own word and not a smoothing. Chronology is what gives this entry its value. It appears two months after the King Follett Discourse (kfd-1844) and nine days before the Sermon in the Grove (sermon-grove-1844) — so before Joseph Smith's most explicit surviving statement of the Father's Father, hostile insiders already understood “a plurality of Gods above the God of this universe” to be what was being taught in Nauvoo. The paper was destroyed by order of the Nauvoo city council the following week; a single issue exists.

title: Sermon in the Grove
speaker: Joseph Smith
venue: East grove near the temple, Nauvoo

witnesses.note: Primary contemporaneous report.

quotes.excerpt: If Jesus Christ was the Son of God, and John discovered that God the Father of Jesus Christ had a Father, you may suppose that He had a Father also. Where was there ever a son without a father?
quotes.note: Unambiguously Father-referent, and exegetical rather than visionary: the claim is derived from a reading of Revelation 1:6 ("God and his Father"), not asserted from revelation. The epistemic register matters for how later sources handle it.

notes: The clearest Father-referent backward-explicit statement in Joseph Smith's corpus, though no longer the earliest — see the 30 January 1842 discourse. Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith 370–73 is an amalgamated citation of these witnesses. Every later correlated BACKWARD-EXPLICIT text traces to this sermon, which is why collapsing citations leaves the backward-explicit column empty after 1844.

title: Eliza R. Snow, “O My Father”
speaker: Eliza R. Snow
office: Secretary, Female Relief Society of Nauvoo
venue: Poem published in Times and Seasons; hymn in continuous use since

quotes.excerpt: In the heav'ns are parents single? No, the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason; truth eternal Tells me I've a mother there.
quotes.note: Affirms a Mother in Heaven and premortal parentage; states no generative mechanism.

notes: Tightened in v2 to HEAVENLY-MOTHER only — the spirit-birth tag was retrojection. The hymn has anchored Heavenly Mother in lived worship for 180 years while leaving the mechanism unstated, which makes it the template for the later euphemism strategy. Verify inclusion and numbering in the current hymnal rollout (Hymns — For Home and Church, 2024–), which supersedes the 1985 hymnal's no. 292.

title: Orson Pratt on the trail: how the first God was formed
speaker: Orson Pratt, as recorded by Wilford Woodruff
venue: Wilford Woodruff pioneer-trail journal, 26 June 1847, quoted at length in William V. Smith, The King Follett Sermon: A Biography, 117–18

quotes.excerpt: One of the most important items if true was presented by Professor Pratt… It was upon the subject of the original formation of the first God; we all admitted in the first place that which we believed to be an important truth ie the eternal duration of matter spirit, intelligence in some form or other we also agreed in the opinion that neither God nor man always had from all eternity the same formation that they now have but did exhist in some form… then the question arose how did God recieve his present formation the answer given by Professor Pratt was something in the following language.
quotes.note: The question as Woodruff frames it is “the original formation of the first God” — a first God is presupposed, which is the exact negation of the chain. Untagged: the available category set has no tag for a terminating chain, and INFINITE-CHAIN would state the opposite of what the passage says. Woodruff's spellings are preserved.

quotes.excerpt: An eternity was filled as it were with particules of intelligences who had their agency, two of these particles in the process of time might have joined their interest together exchanged ideas & found by persueing this course that they gained double strength to what one particle of intelligence would have & afterwards were joined by other particles & continued untill they organized a combination or body though through a long process & as they had power over other intelligences in consequence of their combination, organization & strength and in process of time this being—or God seeing the advantage of such an organization desired company or a companion and having some experience got to work & organized other beings by prevailing on intelligences to come together… it was found to be the most expeditious & best way to recieve there formations or bodies either spiritual or temporal [was] through the womb.
quotes.note: An emergentist account of godhood: intelligences coalesce into ever-larger organizations until one attains sufficient power to organize others. The tail of it — bodies “either spiritual or temporal” received “through the womb” — is the viviparous mechanism Pratt would systematize in The Seer six years later. The bracketed [was] is W. V. Smith's editorial supply.

notes: Woodruff's own diary entry for the day, recording a conversation he took part in while walking with Orson Pratt and Albert Carrington on the pioneer trail. Hearsay D rather than C: the record is contemporaneous, but Woodruff is reconstructing from memory and says so — “the answer given by Professor Pratt was something in the following language.” Pratt offered these ideas as speculation for discussion, not as doctrine, and presenting the passage as his settled position misreads the setting entirely. The contrast that makes this entry worth having: the same Orson Pratt publishes the opposite six years later in The Seer, insisting there could be no first world in the succession and no first Father in the genealogy (see pratt-seer). Counter-cult compilations file the two texts in opposite sections of the same list without noticing they are one man changing his mind between 1847 and 1853, which is also the interval in which he moved from trail speculation to a printed apostolic system. Text verified verbatim against W. V. Smith's block quotation of the diary; the Kenney edition reference (Wilford Woodruff's Journal 3:216–17) that usually accompanies this passage could not be independently confirmed and is therefore not asserted in the venue line.

title: Orson Pratt, “Celestial Marriage” — generation, Gods themselves, and worlds without number
speaker: Orson Pratt
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Great Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 1:53–66)

witnesses.scribe: No reporter credited on the printed page
witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 1:53–66. The speaker did not review the text before publication.

quotes.excerpt: If we were to reason from analogy—if we admit analogical reasoning in the question, what would we say? We should say, that our spirits were formed by generation, the same as the body or tabernacle of flesh and bones. But what says revelation upon the subject? We will see whether revelation and analogy will agree.
quotes.note: The mechanism, and its epistemic status. Pratt reaches viviparous spirit birth by analogy from the mortal body — the same anatomical argument Erastus Snow runs in 1885 and the First Presidency ratifies in 1909 — but he explicitly marks it as analogy and then turns to test it against revelation. Quoting the conclusion without the “if we were to reason from analogy” frame overstates what he claimed here.

quotes.excerpt: …when male and female are restored from the fall, by virtue of the everlasting and eternal covenant of marriage, they will continue to increase and multiply to all ages of eternity, to raise up beings after their own order, and in their own likeness and image, germs of intelligence, that are destined, in their times and seasons, to become not only sons of God, but Gods themselves.
quotes.note: Forward-explicit at full strength: exalted couples produce offspring (“beings after their own order… germs of intelligence”) and those offspring are destined to become Gods. The generative mechanism is not restated in this sentence — it is supplied by q1 earlier in the same discourse — so the viviparous tag is left on q1 rather than duplicated here.

quotes.excerpt: This accounts for the many worlds we heard Elder Grant speaking about yesterday afternoon. The peopling of worlds, or an endless increase, even of one family, would require an endless increase of worlds; and if one family were to be united in the eternal covenant of marriage, to fulfil that great commandment, to multiply his species, and propagate them, and if there be no end to the increase of his posterity, it would call for an endless increase of new worlds. And if one family calls for this, what would innumerable millions of families call for? They would call for as many worlds as have already been discovered by the telescope; yea, the number must be multiplied to infinity in order that there may be room for the inheritance of the sons and daughters of the Gods.
quotes.note: The cosmological consequence: infinite worlds are deduced as the housing requirement of infinite offspring. The infinity here is arithmetical and forward-facing — worlds needed downstream — not a series of predecessors. INFINITE-CHAIN is deliberately withheld.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1852/1852-08-pratt-o-celestial-marriage.md, whose complete text was collated against the BYU JoD volume 1 page scan, pp. 53–66, with print spellings preserved instance by instance (“fulfil,” “endeavour,” “practising”) — the “fulfil” in q3 is the print's, not a typo. Watt-era shorthand report with no reporter credited on the page and no speaker review, hence C. This is the first public discourse on plural marriage published in the Journal of Discourses, which is why the eternal-increase argument is doing polemical work rather than sitting as devotional aside. The reason it belongs in this collection is conflation trap #3 in its purest form: Pratt runs the chain forward to infinity three separate ways — offspring, godhood, worlds — and never once runs it backward. A reader primed for “infinite regression of Gods” supplies the backward half unaided. Pratt here asserts infinite progression, not infinite regression.

title: Orson Hyde: God, our heavenly Father, was perhaps once a child
speaker: Orson Hyde
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference discourse, Tabernacle, Great Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 1:121–130)

witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of the printed Journal of Discourses 1:121–130. No reporter is credited on the printed page; the Watt attribution comes from LaJean Purcell Carruth's Church History Library research on the underlying shorthand, not from the JoD itself.

witnesses.scribe: LaJean Purcell Carruth transcription (CR 100 912, item cr-100-912-0629)
witnesses.note: Scholarly re-transcription of Watt's original shorthand for this discourse, catalogued at the Church History Library. Not yet collated against the printed text for this passage.

quotes.excerpt: Remember that God, our heavenly Father, was perhaps once a child, and mortal like we ourselves, and rose step by step in the scale of progress, in the school of advancement; has moved forward and overcome, until He has arrived at the point where He now is. “Is this really possible?” Why, my dear friends, how would you like to be governed by a ruler who had not been through all the vicissitudes of life that are common to mortals? If he had not suffered, how could he sympathize with the distress of others? If he himself had not endured the same, how could he sympathize and be touched with the feelings of our infirmities?
quotes.note: Two things must travel with this quote. First the hedge: “perhaps.” Hyde does not assert the Father's mortality flatly — he proposes it, nine years after King Follett, as something to remember rather than something revealed, and the chain length is left entirely unspecified. Second the motive: the claim is doing theodicy, not theogony. The warrant is a ruler's fitness to sympathize (Hebrews 4:15 in the background), and Hyde argues *from* the desirability of a sympathizing God *to* His past mortality. Nothing here says the Father had a Father, so no chain tag.

quotes.excerpt: Hence, our heavenly Father ascended to a throne of power; He has passed through scenes of tribulation, as the Saints in all ages have, and are still passing through; and having overcome, and ascended His throne, He can look down upon those who are following in the same track, and can realize the nature of their infirmities, troubles, and difficulties, like the aged father who looks upon his race, upon the smallest child… So with our heavenly Father; when He sees we are going astray, He stretches forth His chastening hand, at the same time He realizes the difficulties with which we have to contend, because he has felt the same; but having overcome, He goes no more out.
quotes.note: The same claim restated without the hedge — the mortality is now assumed and the conditional “perhaps” has dropped away inside a single discourse. Deliberately not tagged DIVINE-PROGRESSION: “He goes no more out” is Revelation 3:12 pillar imagery about permanence of place (the sermon's announced subject is “a pillar in the temple of God”), not a claim about whether God still increases in knowledge. Reading it as a denial of ongoing progression is retrojection.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1853/1853-10-hyde-the-man-to-lead-gods-people.md, whose body was collated page-by-page against the BYU ContentDM scan of Journal of Discourses 1:121–130 (that Final Review also restored the print's British “Saviour” throughout and removed an invented byline a prior pass had prepended). Contemporaneous report in Pitman shorthand, not reviewed by the speaker before publication — hence C. The pulpit research report places the passage at 1:123; that page-level location was not independently confirmed against the page image for this entry, so the venue carries only the verified 1:121–130 range. Value to the collection: this is the hedged, motivated form of the backward claim — an apostle in 1853 offering the Father's past mortality as a pastoral inference about divine sympathy, a full register below the flat assertions of 1844 and 1862.

title: Brigham Young: the gods never had a beginning — “could you have a father without having a grandfather?”
speaker: Brigham Young
venue: General conference discourse, afternoon session, Salt Lake Tabernacle (The Complete Discourses of Brigham Young 2:845–848)

witnesses.note: Provenance as printed in The Complete Discourses: “Ms/219, 81; CR 1234, 48-12, BYC. LJA 12-55-7, 11; TPBY 3:343-6; EBY 86-103; BYA 2:224-237.” Four independent manuscript and print witnesses; the sermon's authenticity is not in question.

witnesses.scribe: Gary James Bergera, Conflict in the Quorum, 125–26
witnesses.note: Independent transcription, used here to resolve words the Complete Discourses scan garbles (“intelligence,” “will,” “born”).

quotes.excerpt: I believe in the eternities of worlds, saints, angels, kingdoms, and gods: In eternity without beginning. I believe the gods never had a beginning, neither the formation of matter, and it is without end; it will endure in one eternal round swimming in space, basking, living, and moving in the midst of eternity. All the creations are in the midst of eternity, and that is one eternity, so they move in one eternal round. Consequently, when you hear philosophers argue the point how the first god came, how intelligence came, how worlds came, and how angels came, they are talking about that which is beyond their conception; about that which never was, and never will be worlds without end. It manifests their folly.
quotes.note: The chain claim in its strongest available form: not merely that gods are many but that the question of a first god is a question about “that which never was.” Referent is ambiguous here because the subject is the gods as a class, not the Father specifically — the Father-referent claim arrives two pages later.

quotes.excerpt: He is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, both body and spirit; and He is the Father of our spirits, and the Father of our flesh in the beginning. You will not dispute the words of the Apostle, that He is actually the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Father of our spirits. You may add these words to it, or let it alone, it is all the same to me, that He is not only the Father of our spirits, but also of our flesh. He being the founder of that natural machinery through which we have all obtained our bodies. Do you wish me to simplify it? Could you have a father without having a grandfather; or a grandfather without having a great grandfather?
quotes.note: Quoted whole and in printed order on purpose. Compilations routinely stop at “…and the Father of our spirits,” which asserts nothing about a regress at all; the regress is the grandfather sentence that immediately follows, and it is the sentence scholarship actually cites. Note also what the grandfather argument is arguing for: Young is establishing that God is the Father of our flesh as well as our spirits — the ancestral premise is doing Adam-God work, not standing alone as a cosmological thesis.

quotes.excerpt: I never heard of one circumstance that varied from this rule, and that was a son of the Emerald Isle who said he was born of one of his aunts. Does this unlock to your understandings how the Lord Almighty is our natural Father; He set the great machine to working. If you cannot see this truth now, you will if you are faithful, and patient.
quotes.note: Kept as context because it names the argument's target in Young's own words: “how the Lord Almighty is our natural Father.” The grandfather analogy is a step in that argument, not its conclusion.

notes: Re-pulled in full from The Complete Discourses of Brigham Young 2:844–848 (digital scan pp. 252–256; the printed pagination of that edition and the scan's own page numbers differ by 592) and collated word by word against Gary James Bergera's independent transcription in Conflict in the Quorum, 125–26, which supplies the readings the scan's OCR destroys. Context that must travel with this entry: Bergera identifies the discourse as Young's “most explicit Adam-God statement to date,” delivered as a deliberate rebuttal to Orson Pratt's Seer series on the pre-existence (see pratt-seer) and probably to Pratt's conference sermon of the previous day; Wilford Woodruff called it “the greatest sermon that ever was Deliver[e]d to the Latter Day Saints since they have been a People.” The same discourse teaches that God is “the Father of our flesh in the beginning,” and later pages carry the Adam-God material proper. Citing the grandfather sentence as a free-standing regress proof-text, without the Adam-God frame, is the single most common handling error attached to this sermon — Blake Ostler's rejection of the chain turns precisely on that frame. Hearsay C: a contemporaneous manuscript report of a spoken sermon, not reviewed by Young in this form.

title: Parley P. Pratt: a plurality of Gods under “one Supreme Head”
speaker: Parley P. Pratt
venue: Key to the Science of Theology (1855), ch. V “Keys of the Mysteries of the Godhead,” pp. 34–36

witnesses.scribe: Third edition (Salt Lake City: Deseret News, 1874), pp. 34–36
witnesses.note: Collated independently; wording identical apart from “firstborn” (1855) printing as “first born.”

quotes.excerpt: It may then consistently enough be said, that there are, in a subordinate sense, a plurality of Gods, or rather of the sons of God; although there is one Supreme Head, who is over all, and through all, and in all His sons, by the power of His Spirit.
quotes.note: The terminus, stated at the head of the argument. Pratt's plurality is a plurality of sons, and it is bounded from the start.

quotes.excerpt: All these are Gods, or sons of God—they are the Kings, Princes, Priests, and Nobles of Eternity. But over them all there is a Presidency or Grand Head, who is the Father of all. And next unto him is Jesus Christ, the eldest born, and first heir of all the realms of light.
quotes.note: The structure is a presidency, not a genealogy: gods ranked under a Grand Head, with Christ as first heir directly below him. Pratt never asks whether the Head has a Head, and never allows for one.

quotes.excerpt: Again it follows, that in the use of this power, by consent and authority of the head, any one of these Gods may create, organize, people, govern, control, exalt, glorify and enjoy worlds on worlds, and the inhabitants thereof… All these are kingdoms which, together with their Kings, are in subordination to the great Head and Father of all, and to Jesus Christ the firstborn, and first heir, among the sons of God.
quotes.note: A clean forward chain — exalted beings create, people and govern worlds of their own — and note that even here the forward extension is licensed “by consent and authority of the head” and stays “in subordination” to it. The forward direction proliferates; the backward direction does not.

notes: Verified verbatim against the 1855 first edition (Internet Archive item keytoscienceofth00parl, printed pp. 34–36) and re-collated against the 1874 third edition and the archive's reflowed copy; the three agree. Judgment call recorded explicitly, because this text is filed in opposite directions by different compilers. Pratt is not a denial of the regress: he never argues against a chain, he simply never entertains one. Nor is he an INFINITE-CHAIN source: what he asserts is a bounded subordination hierarchy terminating in “one Supreme Head, who is over all,” “the Father of all.” In this project's sub-grades that is C-finite — a chain that ends — but the available category set has no tag for a terminating chain, and applying INFINITE-CHAIN would invert the claim while applying nothing at all would hide it, so the terminus quotes are carried untagged with the reasoning here. Reading either an affirmation or a denial of infinite regress into these pages is retrojection: Pratt is answering a different question, namely how a plurality of Gods can be reconciled with the oneness of God. What the same pages do supply, cleanly, is the forward chain.

title: Orson Pratt: “the number of Gods is infinite” — plurality without succession
speaker: Orson Pratt
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Great Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 2:334–347)

witnesses.scribe: Journal of Discourses 2:334–347 (BYU ContentDM page images)
witnesses.note: Collation surface for the vault text; contemporaneous report, speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: …there are many Gods, and that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are Gods, and that all good men in this Church shall become Gods… In these expressions, God has reference to the great principles of light and truth, or knowledge, and not to the tabernacles in which this knowledge may dwell; the tabernacles are many and without number, but the truth or knowledge which is often personified and called God, is one, being the same in all; God is one, being a unity, when represented by light, truth, wisdom, or knowledge; but when reference is made to the temples in which this knowledge dwells, the number of Gods is infinite.
quotes.note: Categories deliberately left empty, and that is the entry's point. INFINITE-CHAIN requires a succession — Gods before Gods, a series with predecessors. Pratt's infinity has no succession in it at all: “God” names one attribute-set (light, truth, knowledge) that is numerically identical wherever it dwells, and the infinity is the count of tabernacles indwelt, a simultaneous multiplicity rather than a genealogy. No backward tag applies because nothing backward is claimed; no forward tag applies because no offspring, mechanism, or increase is named here; DIVINE-PROGRESSION does not apply because Pratt is not addressing whether God grows. Tagging this passage at all would be reading the later framework into it.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1855/1855-02-18-pratt-the-holy-spirit-and-the-godhead.md (“The Holy Spirit and the Godhead”), whose complete text was collated against the BYU JoD volume 2 page scan, pp. 334–347. Contemporaneous report, speaker unreviewed, hence C. This is the collection's essential control. Nineteenth-century “infinite Gods” language is routinely cited as evidence for an infinite regress; Pratt gets to literally infinite Gods by a route that is not genealogical, in the same decade and from the same pulpit as Brigham Young's genuinely serial statements. Anyone citing an 1850s “many Gods” or “infinite Gods” passage as backward-chain evidence has to clear this one first, because it demonstrates that the vocabulary alone does not settle the direction. Two consequences worth carrying: the arithmetic is compatible with a completed, non-successive plurality; and on this metaphysics — God as the finished attribute-set of knowledge, identical in all — there is nothing left for God to increase in, which is why Pratt's opposition to ongoing divine progression is structural rather than stated (his propositional denial lives in The Seer and the 1860 First Presidency exchange, not in this sermon corpus). Structurally this is also the earliest instance of a move the dataset sees again in 1984: defusing plurality by redefining what “God” refers to (see packer-parentage-1984). The rhyme is worth noting; unlike Packer, Pratt is constructing rather than walking anything back, so RETREAT-REFRAME is not applied.

title: Heber C. Kimball: a Father connected with one still farther back
speaker: Heber C. Kimball
office: First Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: General conference discourse, Bowery, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 5:18–23, at 5:19)

quotes.excerpt: We must be grafted into the true vine, and continue to partake of its fatness, and then we shall go back to our Father and God, who is connected with one who is still farther back; and this Father is connected with one still further back, and so on; and just so far as we respect our superiors and try to save our children, so shall we receive blessings from this time forth and forever, and shall become as numerous as the sands upon the seashore.
quotes.note: The chain runs in both directions inside one sentence — ancestors “still further back” and posterity “as numerous as the sands upon the seashore.” One of the cleanest explicit-chain sentences in the Journal of Discourses.

notes: Verified verbatim against the printed Journal of Discourses. Pitman shorthand report; the speaker did not review the text before publication — hence hearsay C under the v2 rebasing of Journal of Discourses material.

title: Wilford Woodruff: God Himself is increasing and progressing
speaker: Wilford Woodruff
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 6:115–121, at 6:120)

quotes.excerpt: If there was a point where man in his progression could not proceed any further, the very idea would throw a gloom over every intelligent and reflecting mind. God himself is increasing and progressing in knowledge, power, and dominion, and will do so, worlds without end. It is just so with us. We are in a probation, which is a school of experience.
quotes.note: Affirmation. The argument runs from the intolerability of a ceiling on human progress to God's ongoing progression — anthropology first, theology second. Later official denials attack the conclusion without engaging this premise. “God himself” is not further specified, hence the ambiguous referent.

notes: The most explicit affirmative divine-progression sentence located in the Journal of Discourses corpus: a full-corpus sweep (~11,600 sermon files, 1830–2026) found no other unambiguous “God is progressing in knowledge” assertion from the pulpit, and none at all after this date. Watt shorthand, not reviewed by the speaker.

title: Brigham Young: instead of inquiring after the origin of the Gods
speaker: Brigham Young
venue: General conference discourse, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 7:282–291)

quotes.excerpt: Many have tried to penetrate to the First Cause of all things; but it would be as easy for an ant to number the grains of sand on the earth. It is not for man, with his limited intelligence, to grasp eternity in his comprehension. … Instead of inquiring after the origin of the Gods—instead of trying to explore the depths of eternities that have been, that are, and that will be—instead of endeavouring to discover the boundaries of boundless space, let them seek to know the object of their present existence, and how to apply, in the most profitable manner for their mutual good and salvation, the intelligence they possess.
quotes.note: Delivered the day after the “never was a time when there were not Gods” discourse (by-chain), in the same October 1859 conference: the same speaker holds the most explicit chain language and the earliest discouragement of the question on consecutive days.

notes: This is the caution the by-chain entry's earlier placeholder pointed at — it belongs to its own sermon (“Intelligence, Etc.,” October 9, 1859), not to the October 8 discourse. The 1997 Teachings of Presidents: Brigham Young manual (ch. 4) excerpts this passage; log that manual as its own citation entry when added.

title: Richard F. Burton: “gods in an ad infinitum ascending series”
speaker: Richard F. Burton
office: English explorer and travel writer; non-Mormon visitor to Great Salt Lake City in 1860
venue: The City of the Saints, and Across the Rocky Mountains to California, ch. IX, p. 388

quotes.excerpt: This body consists of three, viz., Eloheim, Jehovah, and Michael, which is Adam. From the Christian apostles and the Apocalypse, the Mormons deduce the dogma of gods in an ad infinitum ascending series: man, however, must limit his obedience to the last heavenly Father and Son revealed by the Holy Spirit.
quotes.note: Quoted with the preceding sentence attached, because the two cannot be separated honestly. Burton's Godhead is Eloheim, Jehovah and Michael-who-is-Adam: he is describing Adam-God, and the ascending series sits inside that description — the same pairing found in Brigham Young's discourse of 8 October 1854. The second clause is a real observation about how the doctrine functioned in practice: an infinite series upward, obedience owed only to the nearest link.

quotes.excerpt: And as God is perfect man, so is perfect man God: any individual, by faith and obedience, can, as the Brahminical faith asserts, rise to the position of a deity, until, attaining the power of forming a planet, peopling, redeeming it, and sitting there enthroned in everlasting power.
quotes.note: The forward chain as an outsider heard it in 1860, complete with world-forming. The comparative gloss “as the Brahminical faith asserts” is Burton's own frame, not his informants' — he read everything through comparative religion.

notes: Verified verbatim against the Internet Archive scan of the Harper (New York) printing, at printed p. 388 in chapter IX; the 1861 date is the London first edition, and the entry is dated to it while the pagination cited is the printing actually collated. The scan's OCR renders “ad infinitum” as “ad mjinitum” and “there” as “therq”; both are plainly scanner artifacts and are corrected silently. Hearsay B rather than A: the prose is Burton's own published writing, but every doctrinal statement in the chapter is his summary of what Mormon informants told him during his 1860 visit, with no Latter-day Saint source quoted for the regress claim — so as evidence of the doctrine it stands one remove from any Latter-day Saint speaker. Its evidential value is precisely that distance. It shows that in 1860 the ascending series and Adam-God were publicly legible, and legible together, to a well-read non-Mormon visitor who had no stake in either.

title: Brigham Young relays Joseph Smith: a God who had not a Father — nor a mother
speaker: Brigham Young
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 9:286–289)

quotes.excerpt: The idea that the Lord our God is not a personage of tabernacle is entirely a mistaken notion. He was once a man. Brother Kimball quoted a saying of Joseph the Prophet, that he would not worship a God who had not a Father; and I do not know that he would if he had not a mother; the one would be as absurd as the other. If he had a Father, he was made in his likeness. And if he is our Father we are made after his image and likeness.
quotes.note: Three stacked claims in one breath: past mortality (“He was once a man”), the Father's Father (the relayed Joseph Smith saying), and the mother clause — which is Young's own hedged inference (“I do not know that he would”), not part of the reported saying.

notes: The relayed saying is an attribution chain three links deep — Joseph Smith (d. 1844) → Heber C. Kimball (earlier the same afternoon) → Young → Watt's shorthand — so while the sermon is a contemporaneous report (C), the Joseph attribution itself is an eighteen-year-old relay and should be weighed accordingly. Also excerpted in Widtsoe's Discourses of Brigham Young compilation.

title: Orson Pratt: exaltation defined by increase — the angels who have none
speaker: Orson Pratt
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: General conference, Thursday afternoon session, New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 13:183–196)

witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 13:183–196; reporter credited on the printed header. Speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: There is a difference between the classes of angels called celestial, terrestrial and telestial. The celestial angels have not attained to all of the power and greatness and exaltation of kings and priests in the presence of God; they are blessed with glory, happiness, peace and joy; but they are not blessed with the privilege of increasing their posterity to all ages of eternity, neither have they thrones and kingdoms, but they are servants to those of the highest order.
quotes.note: Exaltation defined by the presence of eternal increase, and the definition delivered by subtraction: the ministering angels get glory, happiness, peace and joy, and are still not exalted, because increase is what they lack. Euphemism rather than explicit: “increasing their posterity to all ages of eternity” names the increase and its endlessness but leaves the offspring's nature and the mechanism unstated — the same register as D&C 132's “continuation of the seeds forever.”

quotes.excerpt: We might inquire, have angels not also these affections which belong to the higher class of beings, inasmuch as they are resurrected beings? Yes, but herein they have lost, through disobedience, the privilege of attaining to the higher glory and exaltation. They have affections and desires that never can be gratified, and in this respect their glory is not full.
quotes.note: Context for q1, untagged: it makes no claim about increase itself, but it shows the argument's emotional engine — the deprivation is felt, not merely structural. This is the register in which mid-twentieth-century temple-marriage preaching would later carry the whole doctrine (see eldred-smith-no-increase-1948).

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1869/1869-10-pratt-celestial-marriage.md, whose opening and closing pages were collated against the BYU JoD volume 13 scan, pp. 183–196, with the printed header confirming David W. Evans as reporter. Contemporaneous Pitman shorthand, speaker unreviewed, hence C. Its use to the collection is definitional: increase is not presented as a bonus attached to exaltation but as the differentia between the exalted and everyone else, D&C 132:17 preached as doctrine rather than cited as proof text. Same speaker, same sermon title, seventeen years after the 1852 discourse, and markedly more restrained — the mechanism has dropped out of view even though the entailment has not.

title: Orson Pratt: beget children, form and create worlds, send forth our spirit children
speaker: Orson Pratt
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Discourse in the New Tabernacle, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 14:233–245)

witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 14:233–245; reporter credited on the printed header. Speaker did not review.

quotes.excerpt: Can spirits do this? No, they remain single. There are no marriages among spirits, no coupling together of the males and females among them; but when they rise from the grave, after being tabernacled in mortal bodies, they have all the functions that are necessary to people worlds. As our Father and God begat us, sons and daughters, so will we rise immortal, males and females, and beget children, and, in our turn, form and create worlds, and send forth our spirit children to inherit those worlds, the same as we were sent here, and thus will the works of God continue, and not only God himself, and His Son Jesus Christ have the power of endless lives, but all of His redeemed offspring. They grow up like the parents; that is a law of nature so far as this world is concerned. Every kind of being begets its own like, and when fully matured and grown up the offspring become like the parent. So the offspring of the Almighty, who begot us, will grow up and become literally Gods, or the sons of God.
quotes.note: The fullest forward chain located in the corpus, with every link named in one breath: resurrected sexed bodies retaining reproductive “functions,” literal begetting, spirit children, worlds created to receive them, and those children maturing into Gods. The clause that carries the most weight is the comparative one — “the same as we were sent here” — which declares our own origin identical to the process just described, making the Father a prior instance of it.

quotes.excerpt: We heard this forenoon that, when the Saints come into the possession of their everlasting inheritance and are exalted as glorified and eternal beings, to the increase of their posterity there would be no end. "No end!" What does that mean? It means that it will be eternal--that there never will be a period throughout all the future ages of eternity, but what they will be increasing and multiplying, until their seed are more numerous than the dust of the earth or the stars of heaven… They will not only people worlds, but they will create them. There is room enough to accomplish this when we consider that space is boundless.
quotes.note: Pratt glossing “no end” as a live arithmetical claim rather than a formula — the increase is genuinely unbounded and therefore requires boundless space. Double hyphens preserved from the vault transcription of the printed page.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1871/1871-08-pratt-o-the-redemption-of-the-earthpre-existencemarriage.md, a fresh ingestion collated against the BYU JoD volume 14 page scan, pp. 233–245, with both talk boundaries confirmed directly against the scan and an independent Internet Archive OCR pass of the same leaves. Contemporaneous Pitman shorthand by David W. Evans, speaker unreviewed, hence C. This is the best single exhibit in the dataset for conflation trap #3. The symmetry pressure toward a backward chain is at its maximum here — the process is declared identical in both directions (“As our Father and God begat us… so will we rise… the same as we were sent here”), and the reader has only to run the sentence in reverse to reach an infinite regress. Pratt does not run it in reverse. Nothing is said about where the Father came from, and no chain tag is applied. What the passage does state about the Father is narrower and worth keeping distinct: that He begat us viviparously, which is a claim about our origin, not His.

title: Brigham Young: spirits begotten, born, and brought forth by celestial bodies
speaker: Brigham Young
venue: General conference, Sunday afternoon session, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 18:257–264)

witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 18:257–264. Speaker did not review. No Internet Archive page anchor exists for this range of volume 18.

quotes.excerpt: Mankind is composed of two distinct elements; the first is a spiritual organization in eternity, the second is a natural organization on this earth, formed out of the material of which this earth is composed. Man is first spiritual, then temporal. As it is written in the revelations of God to man, all things were first created spiritual, and secondly temporal. That is, spirits were begotten, born and educated in the celestial world, and were brought forth by celestial bodies.
quotes.note: Gestation and parturition, stated as exegesis rather than metaphor: begotten, then *born*, then brought forth *by bodies*. Three separate physiological terms in one sentence is what puts this past the reach of a figurative reading. The framing matters too — Young offers it as his gloss on the Moses/D&C “all things created spiritual first” passage and as “a part of my own visions upon this matter,” so it arrives as a president's interpretation, not as cited revelation.

quotes.excerpt: Those of the Latter-day Saints who will continue to follow after the revelations and commandments of God to do them, who are found to be obedient in all things, continually advancing little by little towards perfection and the knowledge of God, they, when they enter the spirit world and receive their bodies, will be able to advance faster in the things pertaining to the knowledge of the Gods, and will continue onward and upward until they become Gods, even the sons of God.
quotes.note: Untagged on purpose. This is plain theosis — becoming like God — from the same discourse, and the taxonomy's second trap is that theosis is not by itself a claim about generative exaltation or about anyone's ancestry. Recorded here so the pairing is visible: in one sermon Young states the viviparous mechanism and the deification promise without ever joining them into a chain.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1876/1876-10-young-philosophy-of-man-upon-the-earththe.md, collated against BYU JoD volume 18, pp. 257–264. Contemporaneous Pitman shorthand by George F. Gibbs, speaker unreviewed, hence C; the vault entry is still marked draft, so the two quoted sentences deserve a page-image check before they carry public weight. Chronologically this sits between Pratt's Seer systematization and the 1909 First Presidency statement, and it shows the viviparous mechanism being taught from the general conference pulpit by the President of the Church — not merely written in a periodical by an apostle. The phrase later curriculum inherits is “begotten and born,” and this is one of its pulpit sources.

title: Joseph F. Smith: the exalted man is greater than the angel
speaker: Joseph F. Smith
office: Second Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 23:169–176, at 23:173)

quotes.excerpt: The man who passes through this probation, and is faithful, being redeemed from sin by the blood of Christ, through the ordinances of the Gospel, and attains to exaltation in the kingdom of God, is not less but greater than the angels… in fact having passed from the condition of the angel to that of a God. He possesses keys of power, dominion and glory that the angel does not possess—and cannot possess without gaining them in the same way that he gained them, which will be by passing through the same ordeals and proving equally faithful.
quotes.note: Theosis, forward direction only. The comparison being drawn is between an exalted human and an angel, and the “same ordeals” are the ordeals the exalted man passed through, not ordeals attributed to God.

notes: Re-pulled and read at Journal of Discourses 23:169–176 (discourse “Man a Mortal and an Immortal Being,” Joseph F. Smith, Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, Sunday, June 18, 1882, reported by Geo. F. Gibbs) and verified verbatim. This entry exists chiefly to stop a persistent misfiling. The passage circulates in regress lists — usually cited from its Gospel Doctrine reprint rather than from the sermon — but it makes no claim about God's past, God's Father, or a chain of Gods; its subject is the rank of an exalted human relative to an angel. Under this project's taxonomy it is theosis and nothing more, and treating theosis as evidence for divine ancestry is the second conflation trap. The sentence such lists are actually reaching for — “We are precisely in the same condition… that God our Heavenly Father was when He was passing through this or a similar ordeal” — is not in this discourse at all; it belongs to a Joseph F. Smith sermon delivered twenty months later. See jfs-same-ordeal-1884. Hearsay C: Gibbs's contemporaneous report, published without the speaker's review.

title: Joseph F. Smith: “an eternal being, without beginning of days” and “precisely in the same condition,” in consecutive sentences
speaker: Joseph F. Smith
office: Second Counselor in the First Presidency
venue: Assembly Hall discourse, Salt Lake City, Sunday afternoon (Journal of Discourses 25:51–60, at 25:58); reprinted in Gospel Doctrine, 64

quotes.excerpt: God has a tabernacle of flesh and bone. He is an organized being just as we are, who are now in the flesh… We must go through the same ordeal in order to attain to the glory and exaltation which God designed we should enjoy with him in the eternal worlds. In other words, we must become like Him; peradventure to sit upon thrones, to have dominion, power, and eternal increase. God designed this in the beginning. We are the children of God. He is an eternal being, without beginning of days or end of years. He always was, He is, He always will be. We are precisely in the same condition and under the same circumstances that God our Heavenly Father was when He was passing through this or a similar ordeal.
quotes.note: Both halves, in printed order, in one paragraph. The order matters and is usually reported backwards: Smith asserts God's beginninglessness immediately BEFORE the same-condition sentence, not after it. He puts “He is an eternal being, without beginning of days or end of years. He always was, He is, He always will be” and “God our Heavenly Father… was passing through this or a similar ordeal” in consecutive breaths and shows no sign of feeling a tension between them. Quoting either half alone — which citations in both directions routinely do — manufactures a Joseph F. Smith who does not exist. Both directions of the Father-status axis are stated within this single passage — the same-ordeal claim and the beginningless-eternal-being claim sit five sentences apart; the tags record both.

notes: Re-pulled and verified verbatim at Journal of Discourses 25:51–60 (Joseph F. Smith, Assembly Hall, Salt Lake City, Sunday afternoon, February 17, 1884, reported by John Irvine); the quoted paragraph is at 25:58. Two provenance corrections worth carrying. First, this passage is frequently mis-cited to Journal of Discourses 23:173, which is a different discourse from June 1882 about angels and exalted men (see jfs-angel-to-god-1882) and contains none of this language. Second, the passage almost always travels in its Gospel Doctrine 64 reprint, and it is in that condensed reprint context that the counter-sentence gets dropped. Categorized as backward-mortality: Smith says we are in the condition God was in, which is a past-mortality claim, and he says nothing about God having a Father — so no chain tag. Hearsay C: Irvine's contemporaneous report, speaker-unreviewed.

title: Charles W. Penrose, “The Personality of God”: eternality in intelligence, not in ancestry
speaker: Charles W. Penrose
office: Elder and editor of the Deseret News (ordained an Apostle 1904; later Counselor in the First Presidency)
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Salt Lake City, Sunday afternoon (Journal of Discourses 26:18–27, at 26:23–27)

quotes.excerpt: But, if God is an individual spirit and dwells in a body, the question will arise, “Is He the Eternal Father?” Yes, He is the Eternal Father. “Is it a fact that He never had a beginning?” In the elementary particles of His organism, He did not. But if He is an organized Being, there must have been a time when that being was organized. This, some one will say, would infer that God had a beginning. This spirit which pervades all things, which is the light and life of all things, by which our heavenly Father operates, by which He is omnipotent, never had a beginning and never will have an end.
quotes.note: The anti-regress move, in the one paragraph where Penrose stages the objection and answers it. He concedes that God as an organized person had a beginning, and then locates eternality not in a line of ancestors but in an impersonal spirit of intelligence. Carried as context rather than tagged, because it asserts no ancestry in either direction — that is the point of it.

quotes.excerpt: And if you see a glorified man, a man who has passed through the various grades of being, who has overcome all things, who has been raised from the dead, who has been quickened by this spirit in its fullness, there you see manifested, in its perfection, this eternal, beginningless, endless spirit of intelligence. Such a Being is our Father and our God, and we are following in His footsteps. He has attained to perfection.
quotes.note: Past-mortality asserted as plainly as anywhere in the corpus — “raised from the dead” — but with the eternality predicated of the spirit of intelligence God embodies, not of God's person or lineage.

quotes.excerpt: The person whom I worship I acknowledge as my Father. Through Him I may learn to understand the secrets and mysteries of eternity, those things that never had a beginning and will never have an end. He has ascended above all things after descending below all things. He has fought his way from the depths up to the position He now occupies. He holds it by virtue of His goodness, of His might, of His majesty, of His power… He has won that position by His own exertions, by His own faithfulness, by His own righteousness.
quotes.note: Godhood by self-conquest. This is the alternative to a genealogy, not a step in one: nothing in the discourse says God received his position from a Father, and nothing asks who stood above him.

quotes.excerpt: As the Father had taken His upward course in worlds before this, so Jesus Christ followed in his footsteps in every respect; therefore he is entitled to sit down at the right hand of God in the heavens, to sit on his throne and be one with the Father in all things.
quotes.note: “Worlds before this” places the Father's progression in prior worlds — a real backward claim, and still not a parentage claim.

quotes.excerpt: The individual, the organized person may have had a beginning, but that spirit of which and by which they organized never had a beginning… The works of that eternal spirit of intelligence, the great Eternal God, manifested to us in our Father and through Jesus Christ, never had a beginning. There never was a first world or man; there will never be a last.
quotes.note: The closest Penrose comes to a chain, and it is deliberately not one: no first world and no first man, but no succession of divine fathers either. Structurally this is Orson Pratt's abstract “Great God” — the personages come and go, the intelligence is what is eternal — rather than Brigham Young's genealogy.

notes: The whole discourse (Journal of Discourses 26:18–27) was re-pulled and read for this entry, not just the paragraph that circulates. Verified verbatim. Two things follow from reading it whole. First, Penrose is a genuine backward-mortality source: God was organized, progressed through worlds before this one, was raised from the dead, and won his position by his own exertions. Second, he asserts no divine parentage anywhere in ten pages, and he explicitly heads off the regress by relocating beginninglessness into an impersonal “eternal, beginningless, endless spirit of intelligence” — so the entry carries no INFINITE-CHAIN tag and should not be recruited as one. It belongs with Nelson, Talmage and Widtsoe in the 1884–1915 cluster, where godhood is attained by progression through law from a beginning and eternality sits in impersonal intelligence, rather than with the Kimball–Young lineage stream. Discourse header: Elder Charles W. Penrose, Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, Sunday afternoon, November 16, 1884, reported by Arthur Winter. Hearsay C: a reporter's contemporaneous account, published without the speaker's review.

title: Erastus Snow: a Mother in heaven inferred from anatomy
speaker: Erastus Snow
office: Member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles
venue: Quarterly conference discourse, Tabernacle, Provo (Journal of Discourses 26:213–227)

witnesses.note: BYU ContentDM page images of Journal of Discourses 26:213–227. Irvine reports in third-person indirect style (“Proceeding, he said…”) rather than as a first-person verbatim transcript, so the printed wording is a reporter's rendering of Snow's argument, not necessarily Snow's sentences.

quotes.excerpt: Now, it is not said in so many words in the Scriptures, that we have a Mother in heaven as well as a Father. It is left for us to infer this from what we see and know of all living things in the earth including man. The male and female principle is united and both necessary to the accomplishment of the object of their being, and if this be not the case with our Father in heaven after whose image we are created, then it is an anomaly in nature. But to our minds the idea of a Father suggests that of a Mother
quotes.note: The clearest statement in the corpus of how Heavenly Mother is actually reached: not by revelation and not by scripture, which Snow concedes are silent, but by an argument from nature in which her absence would be an anomaly. That candid “it is left for us to infer this” is the datum — the doctrine is presented as an inference, in a discourse by an apostle, and later usage will present it as settled.

quotes.excerpt: "In the heavens are parents single? No; the thought makes reason stare! Truth is reason; truth eternal Tells me, I've a Mother there."
quotes.note: Eliza R. Snow's verse quoted from the pulpit as the poetic seal on the anatomical argument — see o-my-father. Punctuation and capitalization follow the Journal of Discourses printing, which differs slightly from the hymnal text. This is the earliest pulpit quotation of the hymn located in the Pulpit corpus; roughly fifty talks quote it in all, clustering 1904–1929 and again 1973–1991.

quotes.excerpt: Hence when it is said that God created our first parents in His likeness--"in the image of God created He him; male and female created He them"--it is intimated in language sufficiently plain to my understanding that the male and female principle was present with the Gods as it is with man. It needs only a common understanding of the organism of man and of all living creatures, and the functions of this organism to show the primary object of the Creator, and that is the multiplication of the species… We need only to study the anatomy and construction of the human system, and to understand its powers and capabilities, to comprehend the object and purpose of the Creator, even though the commandment had not been written to multiply and replenish the earth.
quotes.note: Marked implied. What Snow states outright is that the male and female principle exists among the Gods and that human anatomy reveals the Creator's purpose to be multiplication of the species; the sentences about multiplying and replenishing are about earthly generation. Divine viviparous reproduction is the conclusion the argument is built to support and the one his hearers would draw, but he stops at the premise, so the tag is carried as read-into rather than stated. Double hyphens preserved from the vault transcription of the printed page.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/journal-of-discourses/1885/1885-05-snow-e-the-creation-male-and-female-etc.md, a fresh ingestion whose complete text was collated against the BYU JoD volume 26 page scans, pp. 213–227, with the printed header confirming John Irvine as reporter. Filed as an original rather than a citation, with citesId recording the edge to o-my-father: the hymn verse is quoted, but the entry's value is the argument around it, which is Snow's own and is not in the hymn — the hymn asserts a Mother and stops, while Snow supplies a reason, and the reason is anatomical. Provenance caveat, and it is a real one: this is the weakest-fidelity text in the pulpit lane. Irvine reports in third-person indirect style rather than transcribing, so the wording is his rendering of Snow's argument. Graded C to match the Journal of Discourses convention, since the report is contemporaneous and published, but it sits at the bottom of that grade and the phrasing should never be pressed as Snow's ipsissima verba. The vault entry is also still marked draft.

dateDisplay: Couplet as published doctrine, 1880s–1901; origin story dated to 1840
title: Lorenzo Snow couplet
speaker: Lorenzo Snow
office: Apostle, later President of the Church
venue: Published poetry and addresses; origin narrated in later recollection

quotes.excerpt: As man now is, God once was: As God now is, man may be.
quotes.note: The couplet in isolation. Nothing in it settles whether "God" is the Father or the Son.

quotes.excerpt: As Abra'm, Isaac, Jacob, too, First babes, then men — to gods they grew. As man now is, our God once was; As now God is, so man may be... For John declares: When Christ we see Like unto him we'll truly be... The head of all his spirit-race.
quotes.note: Snow's own poem “Man's Destiny” (January 1892). His warrant is 1 John 3:2 — likeness to Christ. The closing “head of all his spirit-race” is a forward-explicit signal: an exalted man as progenitor of a spirit race.

quotes.excerpt: This principle, in substance, is found also in the scriptures. The Lord said to John... “To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne.”
quotes.note: Address of 20 July 1901. The proof text is Revelation 3:21 — Christ's own exaltation. A being who was mortal, is now God, and has a Father above him fits the Son exactly and requires no theogony for the Father. Retagged: Revelation 3:21 describes attainment (“overcame, and am set down”), not mortality — and with referent Son, it does not establish either of the Father.

quotes.excerpt: [The 1840 origin narrative: the couplet received as an insight while hearing Elder Sherwood expound, at Nauvoo, before the King Follett Discourse.]
quotes.note: Survives only through Snow's own recollection some six decades later — hence the D override on this quote alone, while the couplet as published doctrine stays A.

notes: The most consequential revision in v2. Both of Snow's own proof texts are about Christ, so on his own scriptural warrant the couplet is Christological and the Father-referent reading is imported from the King Follett milieu. Counterweight: he dated the insight to 1840 Nauvoo, attributed it to revelation, and his milieu pointed at the Father. Verdict: ambiguous, weighted toward the Son. The consequence for the site is concrete — the couplet should not be read as independent evidence for the Father's mortality; it inherits that meaning only when paired with the King Follett Discourse. That later Church usage exploits precisely this ambiguity (Hinckley's “more of a couplet than anything else”; the 2014 essay's “little has been revealed about the first half”) is itself one of the collection's findings.

title: Orson Pratt, The Seer
speaker: Orson Pratt
venue: The Seer (periodical), Washington, D.C.

quotes.excerpt: Each God, through his wife or wives, raises up a numerous family of sons and daughters... As soon as each God has begotten many millions of male and female spirits... he, in connection with his sons, organizes a new world.
quotes.note: The most systematic viviparous spirit-birth theology published by an apostle.

quotes.excerpt: The Father of our spirits has only been doing that which His progenitors did before Him.
quotes.note: Father-referent and explicitly serial: progenitors, plural, before Him.

notes: A-tier by provenance (Pratt's own pen) but never official, and formally repudiated in part — see the 1865 First Presidency statement, the first official retreat in this dataset, 132 years before the Hinckley interviews. Pratt's systematization is the high-water mark from which the correlated era slowly walks back.

title: First Presidency and Quorum of the Twelve, statement on The Seer
speaker: Brigham Young, Heber C. Kimball, Daniel H. Wells, and the Twelve
venue: Published declaration, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: [Among the propositions from The Seer condemned by the First Presidency and Twelve: that “the father and the son do not progress in knowledge and wisdom, because they already know all things past, present and to come,” and that “none of the gods know more than another and none are progressing in knowledge.”]
quotes.note: Itemization per Eugene England, “Perfection and Progression,” BYU Studies 29/3 (1989), 39. Note the inversion: the earliest official condemnation in this collection protects the affirmation of divine progression by condemning Orson Pratt's denial of it. Exact declaration wording still needs pulling from the original printing.

notes: Added in v2. The earliest official retreat in the collection, and a useful corrective to any narrative that treats doctrinal walk-back as a late-twentieth-century phenomenon. Verify the exact date, wording, and publication venue. Partially filled from England's published itemization of the condemned propositions; the verification flag stays until the original printing is read.

title: Brigham Young on the succession of Gods — and his caution
speaker: Brigham Young
venue: Tabernacle discourse, Salt Lake City (Journal of Discourses 7:333)

quotes.excerpt: How many Gods there are, I do not know. But there never was a time when there were not Gods and worlds, and when men were not passing through the same ordeals that we are now passing through. That course has been from all eternity, and it is and will be to all eternity.
quotes.note: Succession of Gods, not merely plurality of worlds — this is what the tightened INFINITE-CHAIN tag requires.

notes: Hearsay raised from E to C in v2. Most Journal of Discourses material derives from George Watt's contemporaneous shorthand, edited for publication and in the early years reviewed by Young's office — that is contemporaneous secondhand with an editing layer, not untraceable attribution. E is now reserved for genuinely orphaned attributions. The pairing is what makes this entry valuable: the same speaker holds the most explicit chain language and the earliest official discouragement of the question. Quote verified verbatim against the printed Journal of Discourses 7:333 (page-scan collation). The “origin of the Gods” caution formerly held here as a placeholder belongs to a different discourse — see young-origin-caution-1859, delivered the next day of the same conference.

title: B. H. Roberts: an endless line of Gods stretching back into the eternities
speaker: B. H. Roberts
office: Member of the First Council of the Seventy
venue: A New Witness for God (Salt Lake City: George Q. Cannon & Sons, 1895), ch. XXX, p. 466

witnesses.scribe: Mormon Texts Project transcription of the 1895 first edition
witnesses.note: Independent full-text transcription; collated against the page scan and agrees word for word.

quotes.excerpt: But if God the Father was not always God, but came to his present exalted position by degrees of progress as indicated in the teachings of the prophet, how has there been a God from all eternity? The answer is that there has been and there now exists an endless line of Gods, stretching back into the eternities, that had no beginning and will have no end. Their existence runs parallel with endless duration, and their dominions are as limitless as boundless space.
quotes.note: The most explicit published chain statement by a General Authority in the nineteenth century, and note its logical role: Roberts offers the endless line as the solution to a problem the King Follett Discourse creates. If God was once a man, how has there been a God from all eternity? Because there has always been another one behind him. The regress here is a piece of apologetic repair work, not an independent revelation claim.

quotes.excerpt: D'ye think that you could ever, Through all eternity, Find out the generation Where Gods began to be?
quotes.note: Roberts prints W. W. Phelps's “If You Could Hie to Kolob” in full immediately after the prose statement, as the hymnodic form of the same claim. This is why the chain outlives the prose that carries it: the hymn stayed in the hymnbook long after General Authorities stopped writing sentences like the one above.

notes: Verified verbatim twice over against the 1895 first edition: the Internet Archive page scan (printed p. 466) and the Mormon Texts Project's independent transcription. Chapter XXX is titled “Evidence of Divine Inspiration in Joseph Smith Derived from the Prophet's Teaching in Regard to the Extent of the Universe, Man's Place in It and His Doctrine Respecting the Gods—Concluded”; the passage sits directly after Roberts's block quotation of the King Follett Discourse (see kfd-1844), which is what raises the question the endless line answers. Graded never-official: Roberts sat in the First Council of the Seventy and the book was issued by the church-affiliated George Q. Cannon & Sons, but it carried no First Presidency commission — unlike Talmage's Articles of Faith four years later — and it functioned as a missionary apologetic rather than as a doctrinal standard.

title: James E. Talmage: a God who is Himself progressive
speaker: James E. Talmage
office: Author writing under commission of the First Presidency (ordained an Apostle 1911)
venue: The Articles of Faith, Lecture XXIV, “Practical Religion” (p. 430 in early printings)

quotes.excerpt: We believe in a God who is Himself progressive, whose majesty is intelligence; whose perfection consists in eternal advancement; the perpetual work of whose creation stands “finished, yet renewed forever;”—a Being who has attained His exalted state by a path which now His children are permitted to follow; whose glory it is their heritage to share.
quotes.note: Affirmation — the canonical statement of ongoing divine progression in an officially commissioned doctrinal work. Contrast Talmage in the April 1915 Conference Report (“was once a Man, and has progressed … to His present position”), which is completed past progression, not this claim — the same apostle, sixteen years apart, saying two different things that sound identical.

quotes.excerpt: In spite of the opposition of all the sects, in the face of direct charges of blasphemy, the Church proclaims the eternal truth, “As man is, God once was; as God is, man may become.”
quotes.note: The Snow couplet proclaimed as “eternal truth” against blasphemy charges — a useful register datum for 1899 confidence, three sentences after the progression claim.

notes: Text verified against the printed lecture. The book was prepared and published under First Presidency commission and served as a semi-official doctrinal standard for decades; it is not current curriculum.

title: Nels L. Nelson: how our Father became God
speaker: Nels L. Nelson
office: Professor of English, Brigham Young University
venue: Scientific Aspects of Mormonism; or, Religion in Terms of Life (New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1904), ch. XXVI “How Our Father Became God,” pp. 273–276

quotes.excerpt: As respects the eternal principles underlying His purposes, He never changes; these form the very warp and woof of His divine perfection; but as respects the methods or devices for bringing about these purposes, He changes as the exigency requires; and the variations possible to His invention are practically infinite… It is by reason of this very principle of mutation in God that we perceive all things to be in a state of evolution here on earth.
quotes.note: Affirmation — but a bounded one, and the boundary has to be quoted with it. Nelson's God changes in method, not in principle, and the sentences just above hold that on attaining Godhood “how could He be other than immutable? For change would then imply degeneracy.” Lifting “this very principle of mutation in God” out of that setting produces a stronger divine-progression claim than Nelson makes.

quotes.excerpt: But since by this conception He is made to belong to the same order of beings as Christ, His Son,—the same order, indeed, as man himself,—and must consequently have attained to Godhood or creative power, it becomes a pertinent question to consider how He reached such divine sovereignty.
quotes.note: The chapter's opening question, carried as context because it is routinely quoted as though it were the chapter's answer. Note the original begins “But since by this conception…” — the concessive “But” is part of the sentence and is preserved here.

quotes.excerpt: A sufficient general answer, therefore, would be that God became God because He fulfilled the law of becoming perfect as His Father in heaven was perfect; or, in the terms of science, because He fulfilled the supreme requirements of psychic evolution.
quotes.note: Explicit divine parentage — “His Father in heaven,” a phrase Nelson builds by turning Matthew 5:48 back on God himself — with no chain length stated and no interest in stating one. The gloss “psychic evolution” is the Spencerian idiom that marks this whole cluster of Utah writers.

notes: Verified verbatim against the Internet Archive scan of the 1904 Putnam's first edition (item scientificaspect00nelsrich), reading continuously from printed p. 273 through p. 276 so the page breaks between the three quotes are known rather than assumed: the divine-progression material closes ch. XXV at pp. 273–274, and ch. XXVI “How Our Father Became God” opens at p. 275 with the question and answers it on pp. 275–276. Nelson was a BYU English professor writing for a national trade press, not for the Church; never-official.
