He is one of the few authors in the dataset who is both a backward-explicit source and a divine-progression source, which is precisely why his two claims should not be merged into one: the parentage is asserted, the ongoing mutability is heavily qualified, and neither entails the other.

title: B. H. Roberts, The Seventy's Course in Theology
speaker: B. H. Roberts
office: President of the First Council of the Seventy
venue: Seventy's Course in Theology (five volumes); later The Truth, The Way, The Life

quotes.excerpt: [Roberts's articulation of intelligence → spirit → body: an eternal, uncreated intelligence is at some point organized into a spirit body by Heavenly Parents, and later receives a physical body. Exact excerpt to be pulled from the Course in Theology volumes.]
quotes.note: Placeholder excerpt; the framework needs quoting directly from Roberts rather than paraphrased.

notes: Added in v2 as the actual origin of the three-stage model, which v1 wrongly retrojected onto Abraham 3. Roberts's synthesis is what harmonizes Abraham 3's eternalism with 1909-era viviparism: it lets spirits be literally begotten while their underlying intelligence remains uncreated. Never official, but it became the default framework in twentieth-century teaching. Link out to bhroberts.org for the primary volumes.

title: First Presidency, “The Origin of Man”
speaker: Joseph F. Smith, John R. Winder, Anthon H. Lund
venue: Improvement Era (official statement)

quotes.excerpt: All men and women are in the similitude of the universal Father and Mother, and are literally the sons and daughters of Deity... man, as a spirit, was begotten and born of heavenly parents, and reared to maturity in the eternal mansions of the Father, prior to coming upon the earth in a temporal body.
quotes.note: The strongest viviparous statement in the corpus, and the only one that says both begotten and born.

quotes.excerpt: [Man is] the offspring of celestial parentage... capable, by experience through ages and aeons, of evolving into a God.
quotes.note: Tagged BACKWARD-MORTALITY per the v2 revision, but flagging a tension for review: as excerpted, the sentence runs forward (man evolving into a God), not backward (God having been man). It reads as a First Presidency forward-progression claim — arguably FORWARD-EUPHEMISM, since no mechanism is named — and only yields a backward claim by running the couplet's inference in reverse. Confirm the exact wording against the 1909 Improvement Era text, then settle the tag. Retag resolved: with BACKWARD-MORTALITY retired, this moves to FORWARD-EUPHEMISM rather than onto the Father axis. The sentence runs forward — man evolving into a God, no mechanism named — and never claims the Father was mortal. Confirm the Improvement Era wording; if it does contain a backward clause, move it to FATHER-MORTAL-EXPERIENCE.

notes: Verify quote 2's wording before relying on it; if confirmed it makes 1909 a stronger forward-progression statement than it is usually remembered as being. The February 2002 Ensign reprint is filed separately as a citation — its timing, five years after the Hinckley interviews, is the datum.

title: Charles W. Penrose: the gift of endless, perpetual increase
speaker: Charles W. Penrose
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session (Conference Report, October 1911, pp. 48–54)

quotes.excerpt: One of the grand things referred to by President Smith as in the revelations of God to the Prophet Joseph, was the eternity of the marriage covenant, by which the man and the woman may be joined together according to God's order, and though death may part them, yet in the resurrection they shall come forth to be husband and wife, to be parents of children, to have the gift of endless, perpetual increase, the beginning of their kingdom and their glory in worlds without end. That is real life, the power to continue and the power to produce and to increase, the power of vitality in the spirit and in the body.
quotes.note: Explicit rather than euphemistic: resurrected couples are named as “parents of children,” and the increase is qualified twice over as endless and perpetual. “Worlds without end” here is the liturgical idiom for eternity, not a claim about plural worlds, so MANY-WORLDS is not applied. The Conference Report OCR prints “bv President Smith”; corrected to “by,” a scan artifact, with no other change to the wording.

quotes.excerpt: And those who follow in the footsteps of Jesus Christ, who is now to all purposes like the Father, will inherit similar glory, and it will never fade away, and it will be exemplified in them to the full. The spirit of life will be within them in body and in spirit, and they will increase forever and ever, and like the blessing that comes to our elder brother, Jesus Christ, of the increase of their kingdom there shall be no end.
quotes.note: The forward chain closed against Christ's own case: the exalted inherit what the Son inherited, and the increase of their kingdom is unending. The vault transcription prints a stray period in “elder .brother,” an OCR artifact of the printed column; removed here, wording otherwise untouched.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1911/1911-10-15-charles-w-penrose-remarks-15.md. Conference Report, so A. That file has an unusually heavy repair history — two long passages were scrambled by two-column OCR and were later de-interleaved directly against the archive.org page images (leaves n48–n56, printed pp. 48–54) — but neither quoted passage falls inside the repaired blocks, and both read cleanly apart from the two isolated scan artifacts noted on the quotes. Two corrections to how this source is usually described. First the date: the pulpit report gives 6 October, but the vault frontmatter and the printed session heading place it in the second day afternoon session, 7 October 1911. Second the office: he is frequently cited as First Presidency here, but Penrose was not called as a counselor until December 1911, so in October he was still of the Twelve. Why it matters: this is post-Manifesto, official, and undiminished. Twenty-one years after plural marriage ended, the full generative package is preached in general conference without hedging — which is the evidence that the early twentieth century softened the vocabulary of deification, not the doctrine of increase.

title: John A. Widtsoe: a progressive God, and Many Gods who are peers rather than ancestors
speaker: John A. Widtsoe
office: President of the Agricultural College of Utah (ordained an Apostle 1921)
venue: Rational Theology As Taught by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (General Priesthood Committee, 1915), ch. 6 “God and Man,” pp. 23–25

quotes.excerpt: However, if the great law of progression is accepted, God must have been engaged from the beginning, and must now be engaged in progressive development, and, infinite as God is, he must have been less powerful in the past than he is today. While it is folly for man to attempt to unravel in detail the mystery of the past, yet it is only logical to believe that a progressive God has not always possessed his present position.
quotes.note: Affirmation, and an unusually unhedged one — “must now be engaged in progressive development,” present tense. This is the claim Joseph Fielding Smith and Bruce R. McConkie later call dangerous and heretical.

quotes.excerpt: We may be certain that, through self-effort, the inherent and innate powers of God have been developed to a God-like degree. Thus, he has become God… His Godhood, however, was attained by the use of his power in simple obedience to the laws he discovered as he grew in experience.
quotes.note: Untagged deliberately. This is completed past attainment, not past mortality and not parentage: Widtsoe's God rose from among co-existing intelligences by self-effort, and no Father of God appears anywhere in the chapter. Tagging it backward-mortality would import the King Follett frame Widtsoe is quietly declining to use.

quotes.excerpt: Next to God, there may be, therefore, other intelligent beings so nearly approaching his power as to be coequal with him in all things so far as our finite understanding can perceive… Under this definition there may be a great number of intelligent beings who possess to a greater or less degree the quality of Godhood.
quotes.note: The section is headed “Many Gods,” and this is the sentence that gets recruited as regress evidence. It is the opposite: Widtsoe's Many Gods are contemporaries thrown up by parallel progression from a common field of intelligences — peers, near-equals, “coequal with him” — not a line of ancestors. Nothing in the chapter stands behind God.

quotes.excerpt: Man is, nevertheless, moving on, in eternal progression. “As man is, God once was; as God is, man may become.” In short, man is a god in embryo. He comes of a race of gods, and as his eternal growth is continued, he will approach more nearly the point which to us is Godhood.
quotes.note: The Snow couplet is the only backward-mortality content in the chapter, and Widtsoe imports it as a summary rather than deriving it. “He comes of a race of gods” is about man's ancestry, not God's.

notes: Verified verbatim against a scan of the 1915 first edition, whose title page reads “Published for the Use of the Melchizedek Priesthood by the General Priesthood Committee, 1915” — hence historical-official rather than never-official, though the book was never canonical and is long out of print. Printed pp. 23–25 in that edition carry chapter 6, matching the pagination Eugene England uses. Watch the edition when quoting: the Paulsen and Fisher review in FARMS Review 15/2 quotes the 1965 Deseret Book printing, which reads “if the law of progression be accepted” where the 1915 text collated here reads “if the great law of progression is accepted,” and the surrounding sentences differ likewise. Recorded as a divine-progression affirmation and emphatically not as a chain source: this is the taxonomy's fourth trap in its purest form, a source that affirms ongoing divine progression while asserting no divine ancestry at all. Structurally it belongs with Penrose (1884) and Nelson (1904).

title: James E. Talmage: the Eternal Father was once a Man, by right of conquest
speaker: James E. Talmage
venue: General conference, third day morning session (Conference Report, April 1915, p. 123)

quotes.excerpt: you can't change the fact that He is the Son of that Father, and that Father, the Eternal Father, the Father of Jesus Christ, the Father of His spirit and the Father of His body, was once a Man, and has progressed, not by any favor but by the right of conquest over sin, and over death, to His present position of priesthood and power, of Godship and Godliness, as the Supreme Being whom we all profess to worship.
quotes.note: BACKWARD-MORTALITY, and emphatically not DIVINE-PROGRESSION. Every verb is completed: was once a Man, has progressed, to His present position. The progression is a finished ascent that terminates in Godship, not an ongoing increase — Talmage is here answering the question of how the Father came to be God, not whether He is still growing. The referent is unmistakable and unusually over-specified: he names the Eternal Father four ways in one clause, so this cannot be read Christologically the way the Snow couplet can. “Right of conquest” is the distinctive contribution: exaltation earned rather than conferred.

quotes.excerpt: It was crystallized into what we may call an aphorism, by President Lorenzo Snow: "As man is God once was; as God is man may be". We know that Christ is God, and that He lived upon the earth as a Man. In the sense in which Christ was perfect in His sphere, we may become perfect in ours.
quotes.note: The couplet, and immediately a Christological gloss on it — “We know that Christ is God, and that He lived upon the earth as a Man” — which is exactly the ambiguity catalogued at snow-couplet. Referent ambiguous for this quote even though the entry's referent is the Father, because Talmage's own next sentence supplies the Son as the illustration. Note also the demotion in status: the couplet is “what we may call an aphorism,” not revelation. Spacing around the semicolons in the vault transcription reflects OCR of the printed Report and has been normalized; no words changed.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1915/1915-04-34-james-e-talmage-remarks-34.md, transcribed from the official printed Conference Report and verified against a word-coordinate reading-order reconstruction of the archive.org DjVu OCR (conferencereport1915a, leaf anchor n121); the Final Review pass found no body change needed. Conference Report, so A. The office is given as the generic “General Authority” in the vault frontmatter; Talmage had been ordained an Apostle in December 1911 and was of the Twelve in April 1915. This entry exists chiefly to be read against talmage-af-1899, and the pairing is the point: the same author, sixteen years apart, makes two claims that sound identical and are not. In 1899 he wrote of “a God who is Himself progressive… whose perfection consists in eternal advancement” — present tense, ongoing, DIVINE-PROGRESSION. Here in 1915 he says the Father “was once a Man, and has progressed… to His present position” — past tense, completed, BACKWARD-MORTALITY. Conflating the two is trap #1 running in the opposite direction from usual, and it is how a single author gets cited on both sides of the twentieth-century progression debate.

title: Eldred G. Smith: in worlds without end shall have no increase
speaker: Eldred G. Smith
venue: General conference, second day afternoon session (Conference Report, October 1948)

witnesses.scribe: Church History Library catalog record, Conference Report, October 1948 (call no. M204.1 A1 1880, 1897–)
witnesses.note: Authoritative catalog record for the printed Report; the Church's own online conference archive does not reach back before 1971.

quotes.excerpt: Are you teaching your children to keep the Word of Wisdom only because it is a good health habit, or are you teaching them that by not keeping the Word of Wisdom they are not eligible to receive the knowledge and understanding to comprehend the laws of godliness, and so will be deprived of the opportunity to receive the power of the priesthood, and then not be permitted to enter the temple and thereby lose all the blessings of increase for all eternity? That is quite a price to pay, I would say. We are told they will become ministering angels, and in worlds without end shall have no increase. (See D. & C. 132:15-18.)
quotes.note: Eternal increase affirmed entirely by negation — the doctrine appears only as the thing the unworthy forfeit. Euphemism rather than explicit: “increase” is named and nothing else is, no offspring, no mechanism, no godhood. Note also the chain of consequence being drawn, from the Word of Wisdom through the temple to eternal increase, which is what puts a cosmological doctrine into a talk about parental teaching.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/conference-reports/1948/1948-10-eldred-g-smith-conference-address.md, whose text was collated page-by-page against the Church History Library preservation scan on the Internet Archive (conferencereport1948sa, leaves n90–n93) at 0.983 similarity with no divergence beyond spacing and hyphenation. Conference Report, so A. The printed Report supplies no formal title; the vault's is supplied from the discourse headings. What this entry documents is a register shift rather than a new claim. By mid-century the generative doctrine is preached almost exclusively in this negative, temple-marriage-incentive form: not “you will bear spirit children” but “they shall have no increase.” D&C 132:17 is cited, the entailment is intact, and the content has become an argument for a behavior — which is how a doctrine can remain formally in force while ceasing to be described.

title: Joseph Fielding Smith: “our Father had a Father and so on” — one page after “How God Does Not Progress”
speaker: Joseph Fielding Smith
office: President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and Church Historian (later President of the Church)
venue: Doctrines of Salvation, comp. Bruce R. McConkie (Salt Lake City: Bookcraft, 1954), vol. 1, ch. 1 “Character, Attributes, and Perfections of God”

quotes.excerpt: It seems very strange to me that members of the Church will hold to the doctrine, “God increases in knowledge as time goes on.”… But, how does anyone know? Where has the Lord ever revealed to us that he is lacking in knowledge? That he is still learning new truth; discovering new laws that are unknown to him? I think this kind of doctrine is very dangerous. I don't know where the Lord has ever declared such a thing. It is not contained in any revelation that I have read.
quotes.note: Denial. The section heading standing over this text is “HOW GOD DOES NOT PROGRESS,” and the paragraph heading is “FALSE NOTIONS ABOUT GOD'S PROGRESSION.” The unnamed “recently published article” he quotes and rejects is not identified in the book.

quotes.excerpt: The Prophet says: “If Jesus Christ was the Son of God, and John discovered that God the Father of Jesus Christ had a Father, you may suppose that he had a Father also.” Then he asks: “Where was there ever a son without a father? And where was there ever a father without first being a son?”
quotes.note: Smith quoting the Sermon in the Grove — see sermon-grove-1844 — and quoting the second question as well as the first, which is the one that makes the series unbounded in both directions at once.

quotes.excerpt: Yet we have to pass through mortality and receive the resurrection and then go on to perfection just as our Father did before us. The Prophet taught that our Father had a Father and so on. Is not this a reasonable thought, especially when we remember that the promises are made to us that we may become like him?
quotes.note: “And so on” is the whole regress in three words, and it is offered as “a reasonable thought” rather than as a mystery to be handled carefully — from the same author, in the same chapter, who calls belief in God's progression in knowledge dangerous.

notes: Verified by re-pulling the whole of chapter 1 and reading the section sequence in order: THE GODHEAD, MODERN KNOWLEDGE OF GOD, HOW GOD PROGRESSES, HOW GOD DOES NOT PROGRESS (with FALSE NOTIONS ABOUT GOD'S PROGRESSION, PERFECTION OF GOD NOT “RELATIVE,” SCRIPTURES PROVE OMNIPOTENCE OF GOD, GOD PROGRESSES BECAUSE OF KNOWLEDGE, WILL GOD DESTROY HIMSELF?), then HOW GOD IS EVERLASTING (with GOD IS AN EXALTED MAN and CHRIST BORN; YET FROM EVERLASTING), then HOW GOD IS FROM ETERNITY TO ETERNITY. The progression denial and the chain affirmation are separated by roughly a page of text and six intervening headings, so they are recorded here as separate quotes and must never be ellipsed together into one sentence, which is how the pair usually circulates. Taken together they are the cleanest single demonstration in this dataset that divine ancestry and divine progression are independent axes: Smith prints the chain approvingly a page after calling belief in God's continuing progression “very dangerous.” The chain half is expressly attributed to Joseph Smith and quotes both the Sermon in the Grove and the King Follett Discourse (see sermon-grove-1844 and kfd-1844). Graded never-official: Doctrines of Salvation is a Bookcraft compilation of Smith's sermons and writings assembled and captioned by Bruce R. McConkie, not a church publication, though it has long been treated as authoritative. The copy collated is a reflowed digital edition without the printed pagination, so sections are cited by heading; printed page numbers were not confirmed and are not asserted.

title: Marion G. Romney: a process infinitely repeated in nature
speaker: Marion G. Romney
venue: General conference, Saturday morning session (Conference Report, October 1964)

quotes.excerpt: We all know that like begets like and that for the offspring to grow to the stature of his parent is a process infinitely repeated in nature. We can therefore understand that for a son of God to grow to the likeness of his Father in heaven is in harmony with natural law. We see this law demonstrated every few years in our own experience. Sons born to mortal fathers grow up to be like their fathers in the flesh. This is the way it will be with spirit sons of God. They will grow up to be like their Father in heaven. Joseph taught this obvious truth.
quotes.note: Spirit sons of God growing to the stature of their parent, argued from natural law.

quotes.excerpt: As a matter of fact, he taught that through this process God himself attained perfection. From President Snow's understanding of the teachings of the Prophet on this doctrinal point, he coined the familiar couplet: “As man is, God once was; as God is, man may become.” This teaching is peculiar to the restored gospel of Jesus Christ.
quotes.note: “This process” is the one just called “infinitely repeated in nature,” with the Father placed inside it — a chain is implicit by symmetry, but per the no-retrojection principle it is not tagged INFINITE-CHAIN: Romney never states the backward direction. “God himself attained perfection” is the clearest FATHER-BECAME-GOD statement in the set.

notes: The only located instance in the twentieth-century conference corpus (~10,000 addresses, 1897–1970 plus the modern era) where the parent-offspring mechanism is called infinitely repeated and God Himself is placed within it. Verified against the Internet Archive scan of the October 1964 Conference Report.

title: Truman G. Madsen: an imaginary Joseph Smith on how God became God
speaker: Truman G. Madsen
office: Professor of Philosophy, Brigham Young University
venue: Eternal Man (Salt Lake City: Deseret Book, 1966), ch. “Evil and Suffering,” pp. 55–57

quotes.excerpt: Now the Creeds say that God has always been God. But this well-motivated expression of reverence is a solemn travesty. The truth is infinitely more inspiring: that God Himself became God (whose power now extends in and through all things) by the mastery of the same ultimate and unchanging conditions to which you and I are subject. So, likewise, did His Firstborn Son, Jesus the Christ.
quotes.note: These words are not Madsen speaking in his own voice. They are assigned to a character labelled “The Prophet” in an invented dialogue between Joseph Smith and the mother of a blind baby — see the next quote. The content itself is past attainment plus subjection to conditions God did not create; Madsen does not say God was mortal, and he asserts no chain of any length. The always-God tag marks a denial: the passage calls the creedal always-God position a travesty while asserting attainment.

quotes.excerpt: The dialogue is imaginary, but the ideas are not. The “Mother” poses questions that have been raised numberless times. For every sentence in the Prophet's “replies” there is a first-hand counterpart in his writings or sermons.
quotes.note: Madsen's own footnote 5 on the device, printed at p. 55, before the dialogue begins. Any citation of the passage above has to carry this sentence. Note also the limit of Madsen's own claim: he asserts that a first-hand counterpart exists for every sentence, but he supplies no such counterpart for the “God Himself became God” line — his note there points instead to the King Follett Discourse with B. H. Roberts's footnotes, and to a list of finite-God philosophers.

quotes.excerpt: The rare notion that God is in a sense finite, limited by the nature of His environment, has been taught in some form by such men as William James, A. N. Whitehead, Charles Hartshorne, E. S. Brightman, and A. C. Garnett.
quotes.note: Madsen's footnote 11, attached to the “became God” line. It fixes the genre: this is a finite-God theodicy in conversation with process and personalist philosophy, not a genealogical claim about heavenly grandfathers.

notes: Verified verbatim against the printed text at pp. 55–57 (the dialogue passage runs from p. 56 onto p. 57; footnote 5 sits at the foot of p. 55, footnote 11 at the foot of p. 57). The scan's OCR is poor and mangles “but” to “hut” and “William” beyond recognition in the notes; those are scanner artifacts of an otherwise clear text and are silently corrected here. The framing caveat is not optional: the speaker is a fictional Joseph Smith, ventriloquized by Madsen for a theodicy, and quoting “God Himself became God” as though Madsen or Joseph Smith said it flatly is the single most common misuse of this book. Never-official: a BYU philosopher's trade book from Deseret Book. Adjacent interest for the Roberts/James strand — Madsen aligns his position with James, Whitehead, Hartshorne and Brightman by name.

title: Joseph Fielding Smith: progression “not in gaining more knowledge or power”
speaker: Joseph Fielding Smith
venue: First Presidency message, “The Most Important Knowledge,” Ensign, May 1971

quotes.excerpt: And I am grateful that we know he is an infinite and eternal being who knows all things and has all power and whose progression consists not in gaining more knowledge or power, not in further perfecting his godly attributes, but in the increase and multiplying of his kingdoms.
quotes.note: Denial — the definitive official statement of the only-in-dominions position, from a sitting Church President in a First Presidency message. Note the mechanism: God's progression is relocated into the expansion of kingdoms, i.e. the forward/generative chain.

notes: Smith had argued this position for decades in Doctrines of Salvation (which prints “HOW GOD DOES NOT PROGRESS” roughly a page before “The Prophet taught that our Father had a Father and so on” — denying progression while affirming the regress, proof the two questions are independent). This 1971 First Presidency message is the position's most official form.

title: Bruce R. McConkie, “The Seven Deadly Heresies”
speaker: Bruce R. McConkie
venue: Brigham Young University fireside address

quotes.excerpt: [On the proposition that God is progressing in knowledge and learning new truths, listed as heresy one:] This is false—utterly, totally, and completely. There is not one sliver of truth in it. … God progresses in the sense that his kingdoms increase and his dominions multiply—not in the sense that he learns new truths.
quotes.note: Denial, the sharpest on record. Note the rhetorical mechanism: “God progresses” is affirmed and immediately redefined as expansion of kingdoms — quoting the first clause alone reads as an affirmation of the position being denounced.

notes: Never official — a BYU fireside, not conference. It triggered the McConkie–England correspondence (February 1981), the classic institutional episode of this debate; the denial position entered official channels through Joseph Fielding Smith's writings and the correlated manuals instead. Wording verified against the BYU Speeches text.

title: Boyd K. Packer, “The Pattern of Our Parentage” — plurality deflated to the Godhead
speaker: Boyd K. Packer
venue: General conference, Sunday morning session, Salt Lake City

quotes.excerpt: There is *one* God, the Father of all. This we accept as fundamental doctrine. There is only *one* Redeemer, Mediator, Savior. This we know. There is *one* Holy Ghost, a personage of spirit, who completes the Godhead. I have emphasized the word *one,* in each sentence, but I have used it three times. Three is plural.
quotes.note: The deflation, executed in five sentences. “Plurality of Gods” is redefined to mean the arithmetic of the Godhead — three persons — rather than a class of exalted beings or a succession of them. Asterisks are the italics of the published text.

quotes.excerpt: Anyone who believes and teaches of God the Father, and accepts the divinity of Christ, and of the Holy Ghost, teaches a plurality of Gods.
quotes.note: The conclusion the arithmetic was built for, and its rhetorical function: on this definition the distinctively Latter-day Saint plurality claim becomes something every trinitarian Christian already holds, and the doctrine is defended by being made unremarkable. Compare Rev. 1:6, which Packer cites in passing here and which the 2018 New Testament Student Manual will read in the older, stronger sense (see nt-manual-2018).

quotes.excerpt: The acceptance of this truth does not mean accepting the multiple gods of mythology nor the polytheism of the pagans, which was so roundly condemned by Isaiah and the other prophets.
quotes.note: The boundary drawn explicitly: whatever plurality means, it is not many gods. Delivered in a talk that opens by warning against “self-appointed spokesmen who scoff at what we believe and misrepresent what we teach,” which is the apologetic setting the reframe is answering.

quotes.excerpt: This doctrine is not at variance with the scriptures. Nevertheless, it is easy to understand why some Christians reject it, because it introduces the possibility that man may achieve Godhood.
quotes.note: Untagged, and instructive for that reason. Theosis is retained without apology in the same discourse in which plurality is deflated — nothing generative, no offspring, no chain, so no category applies. The pattern the entry documents is precisely this: the promise is kept and the cosmology around it is quietly emptied.

notes: Re-pulled verbatim from the Pulpit vault file talks/english/modern/1984/1984-10-packer-the-pattern-of-our-parentage.md, which was diffed paragraph-by-paragraph against the live churchofjesuschrist.org page at a 1.0000 match. Official published text, so A, and still hosted, so current-correlated. Likely RETREAT-REFRAME and tagged as such, with the qualification that this is a reframe rather than a repudiation: Packer nowhere denies a plurality of exalted beings, he simply supplies a reading of “plurality of Gods” on which the phrase costs nothing. The pulpit sweep that surfaced it makes the surrounding fact available — explicit deification vocabulary (“become gods,” “gods yourselves”) appears in thirty-four talks before 1900 and six after, against a far larger twentieth-century corpus, while “become like God” rises steadily to peak in the 2010s–2020s. This talk is a legible instance of that substitution being performed deliberately in front of a general conference audience. Its structural ancestor is Orson Pratt in 1855, who also defused plurality by redefining what “God” refers to; the difference is that Pratt was constructing a metaphysics and Packer is managing an inheritance.

title: Millet and McConkie: God's development “has brought him to the point at which he now presides”
speaker: Robert L. Millet and Joseph Fielding McConkie
office: Professors of Ancient Scripture, Brigham Young University
venue: The Life Beyond (Salt Lake City: Bookcraft, 1986), 148–49

witnesses.scribe: David L. Paulsen and R. Dennis Fisher, FARMS Review 15/2 (2003), 429–30 n. 22
witnesses.note: Quotes the passage in full with page citation, and states its function: Millet and McConkie “argue for the same understanding of this attribute as do Bruce R. McConkie and Joseph Fielding Smith.”

witnesses.scribe: Eugene England, “Perfection and Progression,” BYU Studies 29/3 (1989), n. 42
witnesses.note: Recorded as quoting the same passage to the same effect. The archive's scan of that issue is too badly OCR'd to re-collate, so England is listed as a witness rather than as a second verification.

quotes.excerpt: Our Father's development and progression over an infinitely long period of time has brought him to the point at which he now presides as God Almighty, He who is omnipotent, omniscient, and, by means of his Holy Spirit, omnipresent: he has all power, all knowledge, and is, through the Light of Christ, in and through all things.
quotes.note: Denial, not affirmation. The verb is the tell: development “has brought him to the point at which he now presides,” and the payoff clause is “he has all power, all knowledge.” The progression is finished. Note also that “over an infinitely long period of time” is a claim about duration, not about a line of ancestors — the sentence contains no Father of God and no chain.

notes: The book itself is not in the collated corpus; the text was verified verbatim against Paulsen and Fisher's block quotation with page citation in the FARMS Review 15/2 (2003), 429–30 n. 22, where the note runs across the two printed pages. Recorded here because the sentence circulates as regress evidence when both scholarly sources that quote it read it as the opposite — a divine-progression denial, placing Millet and McConkie with Bruce R. McConkie and Joseph Fielding Smith against the Brigham Young–Woodruff–Roberts–Widtsoe side of the intra-LDS debate. Under this project's taxonomy it belongs outside category C entirely. Never-official: a Bookcraft trade book by two BYU religion faculty.

title: Teachings of Presidents of the Church: Brigham Young, ch. 4, “Knowing and Honoring the Godhead”
speaker: Church Curriculum Department, quoting Brigham Young
venue: Teachings of Presidents of the Church: Brigham Young (1997), 28–35

quotes.excerpt: The doctrine that God was once a man and has progressed to become a God is unique to this Church. How do you feel, knowing that God, through His own experience, “knows all that we know regarding the toils [and] sufferings” of mortality?
quotes.note: The manual's own editorial voice, in the “Suggestions for Study” section — not a Brigham Young quotation. Two things worth separating: it asserts God's past mortality (BACKWARD-MORTALITY under the taxonomy's first conflation trap — this is not a claim that God has a Father, and not a claim of ongoing progression), and it frames that doctrine as a distinctive the reader should feel good about, which is a register the later material abandons.

quotes.excerpt: Instead of inquiring after the origin of Gods—instead of trying to explore the depths of eternities that have been, that are, and that will be, instead of endeavoring to discover the boundaries of boundless space, let them seek to know the object of their present existence, and how to apply, in the most profitable manner for their mutual good and salvation, the intelligence they possess. Let them seek to know and thoroughly understand things within their reach, and to make themselves well acquainted with the object of their being here, by diligently seeking unto a super-power for information and by the careful study of the best books.
quotes.note: Excerpted in the manual and sourced there to DBY, 25 (Widtsoe's Discourses of Brigham Young compilation), not to the Journal of Discourses directly. The manual's excerpt ends at “the best books” and drops the preceding “Many have tried to penetrate to the First Cause” sentences that open the passage in the sermon. Its wording differs slightly from the JoD text logged at young-origin-caution-1859 — “the origin of Gods” rather than “the origin of the Gods,” and a comma where the sermon has a dash — which is characteristic of the DBY compilation as intermediary.

notes: Verified 2026-08-10 against the live chapter; the manual does carry the origin-of-the-Gods caution, so this is filed as a citation of young-origin-caution-1859 as charter'd. The chapter is the pairing itself: within one lesson the manual proudly names God's past mortality as a doctrine unique to the Restoration, and hands the reader Brigham Young telling them not to inquire after where the Gods came from. That is the modern settlement in miniature, printed in 1997 — affirm the past-mortality datum, decline the genealogy — and it is worth noting that the decline is voiced by the same president who elsewhere pressed the chain hardest (see by-chain, delivered the day before the caution in the same 1859 conference). Hearsay A as a correlated manual; the Young material inside it is C-tier at origin (Watt shorthand) and passes through a second compiler before reaching this page.

title: Henry B. Eyring, “Do Not Delay”

title: Sheri L. Dew, “Are We Not All Mothers?”
speaker: Sheri L. Dew

quotes.note: “Mother” is italicized in print. Two things make this less veiled than the conference norm: “increase” is given an object (“in posterity”), and the exalted woman is defined by motherhood in the celestial kingdom rather than by motherhood recalled from mortality. Useful as a register datum: a general officer addressing women about motherhood is the one modern conference setting where post-mortal maternity can be stated as a defining fact rather than alluded to, and even here the operative noun is “posterity.” The address's larger argument — that every woman is a mother by nature regardless of mortal childbearing — is what the sentence serves, so read it as pastoral before cosmological.
